subject: Culture
title: Sati and Self-Immolation
description: A short lesson to help you apply Sati and Self-Immolation.

hook.text: In 1829, the British banned sati—the practice of a widow burning on her husband's funeral pyre—in India.

buildup.text: Sati was glorified in some Hindu texts as the ultimate act of wifely devotion. Stones marked sati sites as sacred.

discovery.text: Ram Mohan Roy, an Indian reformer, led the campaign against sati before the British ban. Indians fought it first.

twist.text: Many sati cases involved coercion. Families pushed widows onto pyres to claim inheritance.

climax.text: As recently as 1987, a sati case occurred in Rajasthan, showing that legal bans don't erase cultural pressure.

punchline.text: A ritual can be sacred and violent at the same time.

quiz.question: Who led the Indian campaign against sati?

details.summary: Sati — the practice of a widow immolating herself on her husband's funeral pyre — was practiced in parts of India for centuries. Framed as the ultimate devotion, it was often coerced.
details.whyItMatters: Sati exposes how death rituals can enforce gender oppression under the guise of religious devotion. Its history raises essential questions about tradition, consent, and reform.
takeaways: Sati was practiced in parts of India, particularly among upper castes
British colonial law banned sati in 1829 with Indian reformer support
The practice was often coerced despite being framed as voluntary

faq.question: Was sati always voluntary?
faq.answer: Rarely. While some cases of voluntary sati were documented, many widows were drugged, restrained, or socially coerced. A widow's alternatives — poverty, shaved head, social death — made 'choice' highly constrained.

faq.question: How was sati abolished?
faq.answer: Indian reformer Ram Mohan Roy campaigned against sati, arguing it had no basis in Hindu scripture. British Governor-General Lord Bentinck banned it in 1829. The ban faced initial resistance from traditionalists who saw it as colonial interference.
